newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Silence covers Australian ski party town.
newsitem.headline: Silence covers Australian ski party town.

text.p: Australia's Thredbo ski resort, nestled high in the Snowy Mountains, is the place to be seen in winter for the chic and the fashionable -- as much for the partying as for the skiing.

But people in the affluent, tight-knit community showed little interest in either on Thursday, overwhelmed by sadness and shock after a midnight landslide ripped through the small village and buried some of their friends and co-workers.

Police said about 20 people were inside the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges when the landslide occurred just before midnight on Wednesday at the Thredbo Alpine Village in the Snowy Mountains, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.

Eyewitnesses reported hearing voices from the rubble shortly after the landslide but police using fibre optic cameras in their search for survivors said there had been no sign of life in the past 15 hours.

"Those cries stopped fairly early in the piece," regional police commander Bruce Johnston told reporters, adding that the laborious rescue operation was a dangerous one and more landslides were virtually inevitable.

Numbed and subdued, tourists and resort workers sat quietly in coffee shops, or gathered on a small ridge 100 metres (328 feet) across from the swathe of mud and rubble which marks where the two lodges once stood.
The nearby ski slopes were almost empty despite perfect skiing weather. Some shops closed their doors for the day.
"It's pretty close here...you have lots of friends, you work together and play together, ski, and it's really sad," local chef Patrick Scott told Reuters.
"People are still in shock. I don't think they quite realise what the effects are going to be on little Thredbo village."
Police and rescue officials formed a human chain as they delicately removed rubble by hand but Sydney businessman Bill Reeve was pessimistic.
"The mud was soggy and soft, it seemed, around me. It would have filled every void," Reeve, 58, told Reuters.
Reeve was staying just near Bimbadeen lodge and said he heard a "roar and then a crack".

Thredbo, Australia's trendiest ski resort, is a clubbish village where everybody knows everyone. Thousands of visitors and extra workers from Australia and around the world fill the valley during the ski season from June to October.
Thredbo Alpine Resorts managing director David Osborn was drawn and shaken as he told a news conference 15 of his workers, including Americans, are believed to be among the missing.

The landslide gouged a chunk 200 metres (650 feet) by 50 metres out of the mountain on the east side of the valley, dumping tonnes of dirt, rock and gum trees on to the Carinya lodge, sending it cascading on to the second, Bimbadeen.
Debris littered the mountainside and a number of cars were perched precariously at the top of the rubble. Anti-theft alarms from other cars could be heard coming from beneath the debris.
"It looks like someone has taken a great big bulldozer and just drove over both the lodges and they just slid down the hill," one unidentified witness told reporters.

Around town, in the restaurants and shops that stayed open on Thursday, notes were put up advertising a grief counselling service set up by authorities. Some people were readying to leave their devastated playground.
"It's a bit hard to go on skiing knowing this has happened," Lakshman Jayaran, 28, told Reuters as he prepared to make the five-hour drive back to Sydney.
